# Storage Classes {.unnumbered}

The words you may put in front of a declaration: `auto`, `register`, `static`, `extern`.

They control **lifetime** (how long the storage exists) and **linkage** (whether another file can reach the name) — except `register`, which controls neither and does only one thing, below. For scope itself see [Scope and lifetime](scope.qmd).

## The table

| Written | Where it is legal | Lifetime | Another file can reach it |
|---|---|---|---|
| *(nothing)*, in a block | in a block | until the block ends | no |
| *(nothing)*, at file level | at file level | whole program | **yes** |
| `auto` | in a block | until the block ends | no |
| `register` | in a block, or on a parameter | until the block ends | no |
| `static` | in a block | **whole program** | no |
| `static` | at file level | whole program | **no** |
| `extern` | at file level, or in a block | whole program | names something defined elsewhere |

`static` is the one to watch: the same word does two different jobs depending on where it is written.

## What you get for free: zero

| Declared | With no initialiser, starts as |
|---|---|
| at file level | **0** |
| `static`, anywhere | **0** |
| ordinary local in a block | **indeterminate — anything at all** |

```c
#include <stdio.h>
int g;                       /* file level  */
static int s;                /* file static */
void f(void){ static int k; printf("  static local k=%d\n", k); }
int main(void){
    printf("  global g=%d   file-static s=%d\n", g, s);
    f();
    return 0;
}
```

```
  global g=0   file-static s=0
  static local k=0
```

A plain local gets no such promise. `int sum; for (…) sum += a[i];` is a bug: `sum` did not start at zero.

## static on a local

```c
#include <stdio.h>

void counter(void){
    static int calls = 0;    /* created once, survives every return */
    int fresh = 0;           /* new each call                       */
    calls++; fresh++;
    printf("calls=%d fresh=%d\n", calls, fresh);
}

int main(void){ counter(); counter(); counter(); return 0; }
```

```
calls=1 fresh=1
calls=2 fresh=1
calls=3 fresh=1
```

| `static` on … | does |
|---|---|
| a **local** variable | keeps the value between calls |
| a **file-level** variable or function | hides the name from other files |

::: {.callout-warning}
**A `static` initialiser must be a constant.** It is set up before `main` begins, not on first entry, so it cannot call anything:

```c
static int x = f();        /* error: initializer element is not a compile-time constant */
static int n = size;       /* same, even if size is a variable in scope */
```

This surprises people coming from C++, where function-local statics *are* initialised on first use.
:::

There is **one** such variable, even in a recursive function — every call shares it.

## static on a function

The more common use. `helper` below cannot be called from any other file:

```c
/* one.c */
static void helper(void){ … }      /* private to one.c */
void publicThing(void){ helper(); }
```

Without `static`, functions have external linkage by default, so `void f(void);` and `extern void f(void);` mean the same thing — the `extern` is redundant on a prototype.

## extern

```c
/* a.c */  int shared = 42;          /* the definition — reserves storage */
/* b.c */  extern int shared;        /* a declaration — "it exists elsewhere" */
```

```
shared from the other file = 42
```

Make it `static int shared = 42;` in `a.c` and the same two files no longer link:

```
Undefined symbols … referenced from …
```

| | |
|---|---|
| **definition** | reserves the storage — **exactly one**, in one file |
| **declaration** (`extern`) | promises it exists — may appear in many files |

In practice the `extern` declaration lives in a **header** that both files include, so there is one copy of it to keep correct.

::: {.callout-warning}
**`extern` with an initialiser is a definition, not a declaration.** `extern int w = 5;` at file level allocates storage and merely warns; inside a block it is an error. If you write `extern` you almost always mean no initialiser.

**Define a file-level variable in exactly one file.** Two definitions of `int x = 1;` is a duplicate-symbol link error. Two *uninitialised* `int x;` may link silently on some toolchains and fail on others — including the lab machines, where gcc rejects it. Put the definition in one `.c` file and an `extern` in the header.
:::

## register

A **hint** that a variable will be used heavily. Modern compilers allocate registers themselves and ignore it, so you will rarely write it.

One rule is still enforced: **you cannot take the address of a `register` variable.**

```c
register int x = 5;
x++;                /* fine — x is 6 */
int *p = &x;        /* error: address of register variable requested */
```

That rules it out for **arrays altogether**, not just arrays you pass to a function: `a[0]` means `*(a + 0)`, which needs the array's address.

```c
register int a[3] = {1,2,3};
a[0] = 9;           /* error: address of register variable requested */
```

The only thing you may do with a `register` array is `sizeof`.

## auto

The default for a variable in a block. As a storage class it changes nothing:

```c
auto int x = 3;     /* identical to: int x = 3; */
```

::: {.callout-note}
**C23 gave `auto` a second, unrelated meaning**: written without a type, it infers one, as in C++.

```c
auto x = 7;         /* C23: x is an int */
```

GCC 15 defaults to this standard, so on an up-to-date compiler that line builds with no flags, while older ones reject it. Avoid `auto` in this course — in either sense.
:::

## Globals: the cost

A file-level variable is in scope for every function below it.

| | |
|---|---|
| any function can change it | nothing records which one did |
| two functions can disagree about its state | the bug is in neither of them |
| behaviour depends on invisible input | the signature no longer says what it needs |

File-level `static` hides the **name**, not the data: a function in that file can still hand its address to anyone.

Prefer parameters in and return values out. Use a global when the alternative is genuinely worse — in this course, almost never.

## Choosing

| You want | Use |
|---|---|
| an ordinary variable | nothing — just declare it |
| a value to survive between calls to one function | `static` on the local |
| a helper function or variable private to one file | `static` at file level |
| one variable shared by several files | define it in one `.c`, `extern` it in a header both include |
| speed | nothing — write clear code and let the compiler optimise |
